intro: This guide helps you lead twelve weekly sessions on “Praying Hyde (For Children),” the true story of John Hyde, a shy, partly deaf young American who went to the villages of the Punjab in India and spent so much of his life praying that people called him “the man who never sleeps.” It is written for children aged 6 to 12, and works just as well for a Sunday school class, a homeschool group or a family around the table.

Each session takes about thirty minutes. Welcome the children and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the week’s chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s short prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes). Because this is a book about prayer, many of the activities are ways of praying, each one a little different, so children discover how many ways there are to talk with God.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand and have paper, pencils and crayons ready; from week 7 you will also keep one large sheet of paper as a class prayer chart. The book tells of the deaths of John’s brother and of John himself, and of a young man who struggled with drinking, so read those parts calmly and simply, never press anyone to share private sins or hurts aloud, and keep coming back to the book’s point that God hears every prayer. The Indian preachers, families and pastors in the story are John’s friends and fellow workers, so speak of them with respect and avoid accents, costumes or jokes about India.

weeks.summary: John Nelson Hyde is born in Illinois in 1865 and grows up in Carthage, where his father, a Presbyterian minister, prays again and again that God will send workers into his harvest, and his mother, a fine singer, teaches him about Jesus. At college John decides to be a missionary, though, honestly, he also wants to be a famous one. The big idea: God hears every prayer, even small ones prayed over and over, and he listens to us too.

memory_verse.text: Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send forth laborers into his harvest.

activity.title: A Field Full of People
steps: Draw a big field of tall wheat across your page, with lots of stalks.
Beside some of the stalks, draw or write people who need to hear about Jesus, such as a friend, a neighbour or people in another country.
Draw one or two workers in the field, and add yourself as one of them if you like.
Hold your pictures up and pray John’s father’s prayer together: “Lord of the harvest, please send workers into your harvest.”

weeks.summary: John’s brother Edmund, who had promised to be a missionary, catches a fever and dies in 1891, and John spends most of a year wondering whether God wants him to go instead. A friend refuses to argue and tells him to kneel before God until the question is settled; the next morning John says, shining, “It is settled,” and in 1892 he sails for the Punjab. Go gently with Edmund’s death and let children who have lost someone simply listen. The big idea: we can take our big questions to God, wait quietly, and trust him to show us the way.

memory_verse.text: I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, here am I; send me.

activity.title: Listening Silence
steps: Sit in a circle and explain that praying is talking to God, and also being quiet with him, as John was on his knees that night.
Close your eyes and, in your heart, tell God about one question or worry. Nobody needs to say it out loud.
Stay completely still and silent for one minute, the leader keeping time, just being with God.
Open your eyes and say together, quietly, “Here I am. Send me.”

weeks.summary: On board ship John finds a letter from an older Christian promising to keep praying until John is filled with the Holy Spirit; John crumples it in anger, then goes back, smooths it out and reads it again. After a few miserable days he asks God to fill him with the Spirit and admits he had wanted to be a missionary so people would admire him. The big idea: when someone who loves us says something hard, it is wise to listen, stop being proud and ask God for help.

memory_verse.text: I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you.

activity.title: The Crumpled Letter
steps: Write at the top of a sheet of paper, “Please fill me with your Holy Spirit.”
Scrunch the paper up into a ball, just as John did when he felt cross.
Now carefully smooth it out flat again, and read the words slowly.
Decorate the edges of your crinkly letter and take it home as a prayer you can pray again and again.

weeks.summary: John arrives in the Punjab at the end of 1892, unable to speak Urdu or Punjabi yet, and at a street meeting a well-dressed man asks the missionary whether Jesus has really saved him from sin. The question goes straight into John’s heart, because there is one sin he keeps tripping over; he shuts his door and prays until God assures him he can set him free, and later says, “He did deliver me.” Keep any reflection on sin completely private: no one should be asked to name theirs. The big idea: we never need to hide our sins from God; he forgives us, makes our hearts clean and helps us.

memory_verse.text: Create in me a clean heart, God. Renew a right spirit within me.

activity.title: Rubbed Out
steps: Draw a big heart on your paper with your pencil.
Inside it, very small and private, write or draw one thing you keep getting wrong. No one else will look.
Quietly tell God you are sorry and ask him to help you.
Rub it out with your eraser until the heart is clean, and write “Clean!” across it.

weeks.summary: John is shy, quiet and a little deaf, slow to answer but with kind blue eyes; when leaders scold him for studying the Bible instead of only the language, he says, “First things first.” His first ten years are slow, some missionaries think him odd, yet he is not bitter, and in time God loosens his tongue so he can preach in Urdu, Punjabi and English. Be careful that no child’s difficulties become a joke. The big idea: God made each of us, knows what we find hard and can use us just as we are.

memory_verse.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.

activity.title: Patient Listeners
steps: Get into pairs and decide who will speak first.
The speaker slowly tells their partner about something they love doing.
The listener looks kindly at the speaker, waits without interrupting or hurrying them, and then says back what they heard.
Swap over, then talk together about how we can be patient and kind with people who find speaking or hearing hard.

weeks.summary: John works among the poorest village people, whom others would not even touch, and he loves them, greeting them with a hug and living, eating and sleeping alongside the Indian preachers. After staying up all night to prepare a talk, he decides to spend a night getting himself ready by praying, and rises early and wakes in the night to pray so often that the people call him “the man who never sleeps.” If children ask why people were looked down on, simply say it was unfair, and that Jesus loves everyone the same. The big idea: like John, we can begin each day with God and ask him to get us ready to love everyone we meet.

memory_verse.text: Early in the night, he rose up and went out, and departed into a desert place, and there prayed.

activity.title: Good Morning, God
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half so it stands up like a little card.
On the front, draw a sunrise and write “Good morning, God!”
Inside, write or draw one person you will meet tomorrow, and the words “Please get me ready for today.”
Take it home and stand it by your bed, so it is the first thing you see in the morning.

weeks.summary: In 1904 John and his friends form the Punjab Prayer Union, promising to pray every day soon after noon “till the awakening comes,” and Christians begin gathering each year at Sialkot. In 1905 John asks the pastors, “Is the Holy Spirit first?”, and the next morning a speaker, probably John, says God has given him no message, the Holy Spirit is named leader, and people confess their wrongs, sing for joy and fill the prayer room day and night. The big idea: keep on praying and let God lead, even when the answer takes a long time.

memory_verse.text: He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray, and not give up.

activity.title: Our Keep-On-Praying Chart
activity.materials: One large sheet of paper and crayons
steps: Draw a chart on the big sheet with six columns, one for each week from now until the end of the book.
Together choose a few things to pray for as a group, such as your church, a missionary, or children who don’t know Jesus, and write one on each row.
Pray for each thing together, and let a child colour in this week’s box for every row.
Put the chart away safely, and bring it out at the end of every session to pray and colour again, watching for answers.

weeks.summary: John meets a tired, worried missionary named Pengwern Jones, takes him to the prayer room at eight in the morning, prays with him until half past three, and then tells him, “Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work.” At Sialkot John prays “Wide, Lord. Wide,” claps and even dances for joy when people find peace with God, and asks his Father even whether to go to lunch. The big idea: praying for other people is real work for God, and anyone can do it.

memory_verse.text: I am the LORD, your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

activity.title: A Prayer Walk Round the Room
activity.materials: Four sheets of paper and crayons (the leader prepares them)
steps: Before the session, write one word on each sheet, “Teachers,” “Church,” “Friends” and “Family,” and put them in the four corners of the room.
Walk quietly together to the first corner and let anyone who wants to pray one short sentence for those people.
Move to each corner in turn, praying at every one.
Finish in the middle of the room by praying John’s prayer together: “Wide, Lord. Wide.”

weeks.summary: In 1908 John prays, “Father, give me these souls or I die!” and asks God for one person a day to believe in Jesus; the mission’s records show hundreds were baptized in his district, work John called the work of “us,” himself and his Indian helpers together. One day, after praying for ten people, John and two preachers find a welcoming family of nine, and John will not leave until the tenth, the father’s nephew, comes in from playing. The big idea: every single person matters to Jesus, the Good Shepherd, and that includes you.

memory_verse.text: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.

activity.title: My Prayer List of Ten
steps: Write the numbers 1 to 10 down the side of your paper.
Beside as many numbers as you can, write the first name of someone you would like to know Jesus. It is fine not to fill all ten.
Read your list quietly to God, praying for each person one by one.
Fold the list, take it home, and keep praying for the people on it, just as John kept asking, “What about that one?”

weeks.summary: John kneels to pray for an Indian pastor who has grown cold, but starts complaining about him instead, until he feels as if a finger is laid on his lips and hears that the pastor is “the apple of mine eye.” He asks forgiveness, prays, “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother’s life,” and spends his prayer time thanking God for the pastor, who soon after is preaching again “with fire.” The big idea: instead of grumbling about people, we can ask God to show us what is good in them and thank him for it.

memory_verse.text: I thank my God whenever I remember you.

activity.title: Lovely Things Round the Circle
steps: Each child writes their own name at the top of a sheet of paper.
Pass the papers round the circle, and on each one write one kind, true, lovely thing about that person. The leader checks that every comment is kind.
When your own paper comes back, read it quietly.
Go round the circle and thank God for the person on your right by name: “Thank you, God, for…”

weeks.summary: A young man called J. N., from a high-caste Hindu family, believes in Jesus, then turns away and falls into drinking too much; John welcomes him like the father in the story of the lost son, even when J. N. steals and sells his clothes. When J. N. leaves on a train, John weeps at the window; the next day J. N. comes back saying, “I could not forget his tears,” and finds John praying for exactly that. Describe the drinking and stealing simply, without detail, and be honest that his story did not have a neat ending. The big idea: Jesus never stops loving us when we get things wrong again and again, and he helps us love others that way.

memory_verse.text: We love Him, because he first loved us.

activity.title: The Father Who Ran
steps: Tell, in your own words, Jesus’ story of the son who left home and the father who ran to welcome him back.
Choose one child to be the son and one to be the father, while everyone else is the watching village.
Mime the story without words: the son walking away, sitting sadly far off, and slowly turning for home.
Mime the father spotting him, running to meet him and giving him a big hug, while the village cheers.
Sit down and talk about how John loved J. N. like that father, and how Jesus loves us.

weeks.summary: Worn out, John leaves India very ill in 1911; in Wales he tells a deaf old lady to praise God and use church to pray for the preacher and for each person she can see, and she later says it changed her life. He dies in America on 17 February 1912, aged forty-six, telling his sister, “It’s just victory, victory, victory,” and his last words, in Punjabi, mean “Shout the victory of Jesus Christ!” Talk about John’s death calmly and hopefully, and be ready for some children to think of someone they have lost. The big idea: John wanted people to look at Jesus and pray, and Jesus has won the victory for everyone who trusts him.

memory_verse.text: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

activity.title: Look and Pray, Then Shout
activity.materials: Nothing (and the class prayer chart from week 7)
steps: Sit in a circle with your eyes open, just like the deaf lady in church.
Look at each person round the circle, one at a time, and silently pray a short blessing for them.
Bring out the prayer chart, colour in the last boxes, and thank God for any answers you have seen.
Stand up together and shout John’s last words in English: “Shout the victory of Jesus Christ!”
